analogy.p: Think of the metal and carbon as two people pulling on the same rope, the rope being the oxygen atoms. If carbon is stronger (more reactive) than the metal, carbon wins the oxygen and the metal is left on its own, which is how carbon extracts iron or zinc. If the metal is stronger than carbon, as aluminium is, carbon cannot win and you need an outside force, electricity, to rip the oxygen away. It breaks down because real chemical bonds are not just a matter of strength: temperature, energy and which products form (CO or CO2) all matter.

bullets: **Ore:** a rock containing enough metal (or metal compound) to make extraction **economically viable**; what counts as an ore changes with the price of the metal and the cost of extracting it.
Most ores contain the metal combined with oxygen as a **metal oxide**, for example iron(III) oxide (haematite) Fe2O3, aluminium oxide (in bauxite) Al2O3 and zinc oxide.
**Native metals:** gold (and sometimes silver and copper) can be found as the element because they do not react with air or water, so little chemical extraction is needed.
Reactive metals form **stable compounds**, so they are hard to separate from their ores and need more energy-intensive methods.
Extraction = turning a metal compound in an ore into the free metal. Chemically this is a **reduction** because the metal ion gains electrons or the oxide loses oxygen.
A metal's **position in the reactivity series** tells you which extraction method is possible.
Ores are non-renewable resources: they are used up faster than they form.
core.h: Where metals come from: ores and native metals
core.p: Most metals are found in the Earth's crust combined with other elements, usually as **oxides** or sulfides, and must be chemically separated before they can be used. A rock that contains enough metal or metal compound to make it **economically worthwhile to extract the metal** is called an **ore**. A few very unreactive metals, such as **gold**, are found as the uncombined element (they occur **native**), so they just need to be separated from the rock. How a metal is extracted depends entirely on how reactive it is, which is why this topic follows directly from the reactivity series.

bullets: **Mining:** surface (open-cast quarrying) or underground. It destroys habitats, produces dust and noise and leaves large amounts of waste rock (spoil).
**Concentrating the ore:** separating the metal-containing mineral from the rest of the rock (for example by crushing and flotation) so that less material has to be processed.
**Extraction:** chemical reaction (reduction with carbon, or electrolysis) to separate the metal from its compound.
**Purification:** removing impurities to give a metal of the required quality; impurities can make metals brittle or reduce conductivity.
Only **high-grade** or sufficiently rich ores are used if extraction is expensive; **low-grade ores** need new methods such as bioleaching or phytomining.
Costs include energy, transport, labour and disposing of waste; benefits are the value of the metal.
Link to **sustainability**: using metals efficiently and recycling reduces mining, saves energy and conserves ore.
core.h: Ores are mined, concentrated and purified
core.p: Extraction is a multi-stage industrial process. The ore must first be **mined** from the ground, then often **concentrated** to remove unwanted rock (waste material), and only then is the metal chemically extracted. The extracted metal may finally need **purification** before it can be used. Each stage uses energy and money, and the environmental cost of mining is a key reason why recycling metals is so important.

bullets: **Above carbon (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al):** extracted by electrolysis of the molten compound; this is expensive because of the large amount of electrical energy needed.
**Below carbon (Zn, Fe, Cu and others such as tin and lead):** extracted by reduction with carbon (heating the oxide with carbon or carbon monoxide); cheaper and carbon is readily available as coke.
**Gold:** found uncombined, so only needs physical separation from the rock.
Why electrolysis is dearer: the compound must be **melted** (high temperatures) and a large electric current passed through it.
Reactive metals are extracted last in history: aluminium only became cheap after electricity could be generated on a large scale.
Always **link the method to the series**: 'Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it; electrolysis is used.'
Remember carbon is placed in the series for comparison, as a non-metal.
core.p: The rule is simple: a metal can be extracted by heating its oxide with **carbon** only if the metal is **less reactive than carbon**. Carbon is more reactive than the metal so it takes the oxygen away, leaving the metal behind. Metals **more reactive than carbon** cannot be displaced by carbon, so their compounds must be broken up by **electrolysis**, which uses electricity. The line between the two methods is the position of carbon in the reactivity series, between aluminium and zinc. Gold is so unreactive that it needs no chemical extraction.

bullets: General word equation: **metal oxide + carbon → metal + carbon dioxide**.
**Copper oxide:** 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2 (black powder turns to pink-brown copper).
**Iron(III) oxide:** 2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2.
**Zinc oxide:** 2ZnO + C → 2Zn + CO2 or ZnO + C → Zn + CO, depending on the amount of carbon and temperature.
**Carbon monoxide** can also act as the reducing agent: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2.
Always check the equation balances: for 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2 there are 2 Cu, 1 C and 2 O on each side.
Heating is needed to give the reaction its activation energy and to melt or vaporise some metals.
core.h: Reduction of metal oxides by carbon
core.p: When a metal oxide is heated with carbon, carbon removes the oxygen from the metal oxide to form carbon dioxide (or carbon monoxide), and the metal is left behind. The metal oxide is **reduced** because it loses oxygen, and the carbon is **oxidised** because it gains oxygen. This works because carbon is more reactive than the metal; it is a displacement reaction in which carbon displaces the metal from its oxide. High temperatures are needed to start and sustain the reaction.

bullets: **Reduction = loss of oxygen** (metal oxide → metal).
**Oxidation = gain of oxygen** (carbon → carbon dioxide, or carbon monoxide → carbon dioxide).
In Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2: iron(III) oxide is reduced; carbon monoxide is oxidised.
In terms of electrons: metal ions in the oxide **gain electrons** (reduction), carbon atoms **lose electrons** (oxidation).
The substance that is oxidised is the **reducing agent** (carbon, CO); the one that is reduced is the **oxidising agent** (the metal oxide).
Method: look at what has lost oxygen (reduced) and what has gained it (oxidised); quote the species by name in your answer.
Link: the same OIL RIG electron ideas as the displacement reactions in the reactivity series note.
core.h: Oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen
core.p: In extraction reactions the definitions used are in terms of oxygen: **reduction is loss of oxygen** and **oxidation is gain of oxygen**. In the reaction 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2, copper oxide loses oxygen so it is reduced; carbon gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide so it is oxidised. Whenever there is reduction there is also oxidation, so these are **redox reactions**. Higher tier questions may give an unfamiliar equation and ask you to identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced and to justify using oxygen.

bullets: Carbon is below aluminium in the series, so **Al2O3 + C → no reaction**.
The metal ions are held very strongly in the compound, so a stronger method (electrolysis) is needed.
Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point, so it is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the temperature needed and save energy.
In electrolysis, metal ions are reduced by **gaining electrons at the negative electrode**.
The extraction of aluminium is covered in its own note; the key idea is that electrolysis is used for metals above carbon.
Higher tier: explain why a more reactive metal is not formed by displacement with carbon, using the position of carbon in the series.
Cost: electrolysis uses a lot of electricity, making aluminium and other reactive metals more expensive per tonne than iron.
core.h: Why carbon cannot extract reactive metals
core.p: Carbon can only take oxygen from the oxide of a metal that is **less reactive than carbon**. Reactive metals such as aluminium, magnesium and sodium hold on to oxygen much more strongly than carbon does, so carbon is not able to displace them. Their compounds are very stable and need a much bigger energy input, supplied by passing electricity through the molten compound.

bullets: Raw materials: iron ore (Fe2O3), coke (carbon), limestone (CaCO3) and hot air (oxygen).
Coke burns: **C + O2 → CO2**, giving off heat that keeps the furnace hot.
Carbon dioxide reacts with coke: **CO2 + C → 2CO**.
**Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2**: the iron(III) oxide is **reduced** and carbon monoxide is **oxidised**.
Limestone decomposes: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2; calcium oxide reacts with silicon dioxide impurities: CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3 (**slag**). Slag floats on the molten iron and is tapped off separately.
Iron from the furnace (pig iron) is brittle because it contains about 4% carbon and other impurities; it is converted into steel in a further stage.
The furnace runs continuously and the temperatures are very high, so it uses a lot of energy.
core.h: Extracting iron in the blast furnace
core.p: Iron is the most widely used metal and is extracted from iron ore (haematite, mainly iron(III) oxide) in a **blast furnace**. Iron ore, **coke** (carbon) and **limestone** are fed into the top of the furnace and hot air is blasted in near the bottom. Carbon burns to make carbon dioxide, which reacts with more carbon to make carbon monoxide; carbon monoxide is the main reducing agent which removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide. Molten iron collects at the bottom. This process is an example of reduction by carbon in industry.

bullets: **Phytomining:** plants are grown on soil containing the metal compound; they absorb the metal ions and concentrate them in their tissues; the plants are harvested and **burned**; the **ash** contains the metal compound, from which the metal is obtained.
**Bioleaching:** bacteria feed on low-grade ores and produce a solution called a **leachate** that contains metal ions (for example copper ions); the metal is then obtained from the leachate.
In both cases the metal can be extracted from solution by **electrolysis** or by **displacement using scrap iron**: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu.
Displacement works because iron is more reactive than copper (see the reactivity series).
Advantages: they conserve high-grade ore, need less energy than smelting, and cause less damage to the land than traditional mining.
Disadvantages: they are slow, take up a lot of land (phytomining) and require suitable conditions.
These methods let us get value from ores that are otherwise not worth mining.
core.h: Biological methods of extracting copper (chemistry only)
core.p: Traditional mining and smelting need high-grade ores, but supplies of these are running out. Newer methods are used to extract metals such as copper from **low-grade ores** that would be too expensive to treat otherwise. They are less damaging to the environment than mining and smelting, but they are slow. The two methods are **phytomining**, which uses plants, and **bioleaching**, which uses bacteria. This content is for students who take the separate chemistry (triple) papers.

bullets: Energy costs: electrolysis (electricity) is more expensive than using carbon, so metals above carbon cost more.

Environmental impacts: mining destroys habitats and produces waste; extraction releases **carbon dioxide** (a greenhouse gas); carbon monoxide is toxic; sulfur dioxide from sulfide ores causes acid rain.
**Recycling** metals uses much less energy than extraction (recycling aluminium saves a very large fraction of the energy needed to make it from ore) and conserves ores and reduces landfill.
Not all metals are equally easy to recycle: it depends on collection, sorting, and how mixed they are.
Economic factors: price of the metal, availability of the ore, cost of fuel and electricity, location and transport, and the value of by-products.
Social factors: mining brings jobs but can disturb communities and cause pollution.
When asked 'evaluate', give a **conclusion** and justify it, not just a list.
core.h: Economic and environmental issues in extraction
core.p: Choosing how to extract a metal is a balance of cost, energy, environmental damage and the supply of raw materials. Questions often ask you to evaluate or compare processes using information given. A good evaluation weighs up pros and cons from both an economic viewpoint and an environmental one, and reaches a reasoned judgement.

bullets: Relative formula mass of iron(III) oxide: Mr = (2 × 56) + (3 × 16) = 112 + 48 = **160**.
Percentage of iron in Fe2O3 = 112 ÷ 160 × 100 = **70%**.
Mass of metal = mass of oxide × (mass of metal in formula ÷ Mr).
Percentage of copper in CuO: Mr = 64 + 16 = 80; Cu = 64 ÷ 80 × 100 = **80%**.
Percentage of aluminium in Al2O3: Mr = 54 + 48 = 102; Al = 54 ÷ 102 × 100 = **52.9%**.
Using moles: 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2 means moles of Cu equals moles of CuO; moles = mass ÷ Mr.
Real yields are lower than the calculated mass because of incomplete reaction and loss of product.
core.h: Calculations: how much metal can be extracted?
core.p: The mass of a metal that can be obtained from a metal oxide can be calculated using relative formula masses and ratios, as in any reacting mass calculation. First find the relative formula mass of the oxide, then calculate the percentage of the metal in it, or use the balanced equation to find moles. Always give units and check that the answer is less than the mass of the ore or oxide, as some mass is oxygen.

bullets: Chain of reasoning: position in series → method → energy cost → price.
If asked 'why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis?': it is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide.
If asked 'why is iron extracted using carbon?': iron is less reactive than carbon, and carbon is cheap and abundant.
If asked 'why is gold found as the metal?': it is very unreactive so it does not form compounds.
Link to **Group 1**: the alkali metals are extracted by electrolysis because they are very reactive.
Link to **corrosion**: iron rusts as it is more reactive than copper; reactive metals corrode faster.
Link to **climate**: heating with carbon releases CO2, so extraction contributes to global warming.
core.p: Extraction questions combine ideas from the reactivity series, oxidation and reduction, electrolysis and the use of resources. To score full marks always make the **link to reactivity** explicit, use the correct definitions of oxidation and reduction, and name the substances involved. Practise writing short, logical chains such as 'zinc is less reactive than carbon, so carbon displaces zinc from zinc oxide, so zinc oxide is reduced'.

exam: **State (1 mark):** definitions such as 'reduction is loss of oxygen' and 'an ore is a rock containing enough metal to be economical to extract'.
**Why is X extracted by Y? (2 marks):** compare X with carbon in the series: 'X is above/below carbon so ...'; then give the method.
**Identify oxidised/reduced (2 marks):** name the species and give the oxygen (or electron) reason: 'iron oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen'.
**Word and symbol equations (1-3 marks):** metal oxide + carbon → metal + carbon dioxide; balance, and check with the atom count.
**Blast furnace description (up to 4 marks):** raw materials, role of coke, equation for reduction, role of limestone, products.
**Compare methods (4-6 marks):** give two or three points for each method (cost, energy, environment) and a justified conclusion.
**Evaluate (6 marks):** advantages and disadvantages of a method, link to resources and sustainability, and a conclusion.
**Calculations (2-3 marks):** relative formula mass, ratio, and units; show each step because marks are for method.
**Triple only:** phytomining and bioleaching need the stages in the correct order, and one disadvantage (slow) and one advantage.
**Use the data given:** in table or graph questions quote values and compare them, for example 'reaction with carbon at 1000 °C'.

mistakes.r: Reduction is **loss** of oxygen; oxidation is gain of oxygen.
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so it must be extracted by electrolysis.
Metals are chemically extracted from compounds by reduction or electrolysis, not just melted.
mistakes.w: The metal is melted out of the ore.

mistakes.r: Carbon is a non-metal included for comparison; it marks the extraction boundary.
mistakes.w: Carbon is a metal in the series.

mistakes.r: Iron(III) oxide is **reduced**; the carbon monoxide is oxidised.
mistakes.w: Iron(III) oxide is oxidised in the blast furnace.

mistakes.r: Limestone removes impurities as slag; it is not a source of iron.
mistakes.w: Limestone is used to make iron.

mistakes.r: Electrolysis is used for reactive metals despite being expensive, because carbon cannot reduce them.
mistakes.w: Electrolysis is used because it is cheap.

mistakes.r: Gold is unreactive and found native, so it does not need chemical extraction.
mistakes.w: Gold is extracted from its oxide.

mistakes.r: Burning plants is phytomining; bioleaching uses bacteria to make a leachate.
mistakes.w: Bioleaching burns the plants to get copper.

summary: You must know that unreactive metals such as gold occur native, that metals less reactive than carbon are extracted by heating their oxides with carbon (reduction), and that more reactive metals need electrolysis. You must identify oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen, and for the triple paper know phytomining and bioleaching. It matters because it explains why metals have different costs and environmental impacts.

terms.d: A rock that contains enough metal or metal compound to make it economically worthwhile to extract the metal.
A metal found in the Earth as the uncombined element, such as gold.
The process of obtaining a metal from its ore.
Loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons).
Gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons).
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together.
A substance that removes oxygen from (or gives electrons to) another substance and is oxidised itself.
The breaking down of an ionic compound, molten or in solution, using electricity.
A furnace in which iron oxide is reduced to iron using carbon monoxide from coke and hot air.
Waste produced in the blast furnace from calcium oxide reacting with impurities such as silicon dioxide.
A form of carbon made from coal, used as fuel and reducing agent in the blast furnace.
Using plants to absorb metal compounds from soil; the plants are burned and the metal extracted from the ash.
Using bacteria to produce a solution (leachate) containing metal ions from low-grade ore.
A solution containing dissolved metal compounds, produced in bioleaching.
An ore containing only a small proportion of metal.
Collecting and reprocessing used materials to make new products, saving ore and energy.

worked.ans: (a) Iron and zinc. (b) Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take oxygen from aluminium oxide; electrolysis is needed. (c) Gold is very unreactive, so it is found as the uncombined metal.
worked.q: The table lists four metals: aluminium, iron, gold and zinc. (a) Which two can be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon? (b) Explain why the other metal in the list cannot be extracted this way. (c) Why does gold not need extracting? (4 marks)
steps: Carbon can reduce oxides of metals less reactive than carbon.
Iron and zinc are below carbon in the series (Al > C > Zn > Fe).
Aluminium is above carbon so carbon cannot displace it.
Gold is the least reactive and does not form compounds.

worked.ans: Zinc oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen; carbon is oxidised because it gains oxygen.
worked.q: Zinc oxide is heated with carbon: ZnO + C → Zn + CO. State which substance is oxidised and which is reduced. Explain your answer. (3 marks)
steps: Zinc oxide loses oxygen to become zinc.
Carbon gains oxygen to become carbon monoxide.
Reduction = loss of oxygen; oxidation = gain of oxygen.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of iron that can be obtained from 1000 kg of pure iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16) (3 marks)
steps: Mass of iron in 160 g of Fe2O3 = 2 × 56 = 112 g.
